units.blurb: Conduction, convection and radiation; browning reactions.

topics.title: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
topics.short: Pans conduct heat into food, air and liquids carry it by convection, and broilers and grills radiate it; most cooking uses all three.
topics.trouble: People think a hotter oven always cooks faster without a cost; the outside overcooks before heat reaches the center.

topics.title: Browning: the Maillard Reaction and Caramelization
topics.short: Above about 280°F to 300°F, proteins and sugars react to make brown color and roasted flavor (Maillard); sugar alone browns as it breaks down (caramelization). Water keeps the surface too cool, so dry the food.
topics.trouble: Cooks crowd a wet pan and wonder why the meat steams gray instead of browning.

topics.title: Sautéing, Stir-Frying and Pan-Frying
topics.short: Sauté: a little fat, a hot pan, small pieces moving. Pan-fry: more fat, often a breading, cooked on one side and then the other.
topics.trouble: Beginners put food in a cold pan with cold oil, so it sticks and soaks up fat.

topics.title: Deep-Frying and Oil Safety
topics.short: Food submerged in oil at about 325°F to 375°F; dry the food, fry in small batches, and know the fire rules: never water on a grease fire, smother it with a lid, Class K extinguishers in commercial kitchens.
topics.trouble: People drop wet or frozen food with ice crystals into hot oil, which spatters and can boil over.

topics.title: Roasting, Grilling and Broiling
topics.short: Roast in hot air, grill over the heat, broil under it; sear, then finish at a lower temperature for large pieces, and use a thermometer.
topics.trouble: Cooks cut into meat to check it and lose the juices; a probe thermometer answers without a cut.

topics.title: Poaching, Simmering, Boiling and Steaming
topics.short: Poach at about 160°F to 180°F, simmer at about 185°F to 205°F, boil at 212°F at sea level; steam cooks by condensing vapor. Water boils at a lower temperature high in the mountains.
topics.trouble: Cooks boil what should be poached, which toughens fish and breaks up eggs.

topics.title: Braising and Stewing
topics.short: Brown first, then cook slowly, partly covered in liquid, until tough connective tissue turns to gelatin. Braises use large pieces in a little liquid; stews use smaller pieces covered in liquid.
topics.trouble: People braise at a hard boil, which dries the meat even though it sits in liquid.

topics.title: Sous Vide: Precise Low-Temperature Cooking
topics.short: Food sealed in a bag and cooked in a water bath held at an exact temperature. Safety comes from time at temperature: reach a safe minimum temperature, or hold long enough by a published table.
topics.trouble: Cooks think a low bath temperature is safe because the food is sealed; time at temperature is what makes it safe.
